angle: Comparative materials-science evaluation of the six major clay cookware families (common red earthenware/terracotta, micaceous/burnished black earthenware, Chinese Zisha, kaolin-rich stoneware/porcelain, LAS/MAS flameware, and 'volcanic clay') measured against the three governing engineering variables: firing temperature/vitrification, open porosity, and thermal expansion (temper/flux/glaze).

findings.claim: Common red earthenware / terracotta (e.g., Römertopf, Spanish cazuela, unglazed Moroccan tagine) is low-fired and unvitrified, yielding high open porosity and water absorption unless glazed or tempered with refractory inclusions.
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Water absorption varies by firing schedule and clay mineralogy: standard earthenware spans >3% to 15%+ per ASTM C373, while unglazed utilitarian terracotta cookware commonly reaches 10–20%+. Traditional Moroccan kilns fire as low as 800–1,000 °C; Spanish refractory Pereruela cazuelas blend red clay with white refractory clay tempered with coarse quartz, feldspar, and mica for stovetop survivability.
sources: ASTM C373 / USITC whiteware standards (austingallery.org)
Britannica & Spanish refractory cookware technical descriptions (tienda.com, ancientcookware.com)
FDA / Health Canada ceramic earthenware reports (fda.gov, cbc.ca)
findings.value_or_range: Firing: 900–1,063 °C (Cone 010–04; traditional tagines 800–1,000 °C); Water absorption: >3% to 20%+; CTE: 5.0–8.0 × 10^-6 K^-1; Thermal conductivity: ~0.15–1.8 W/(m·K)

findings.claim: Low-fired glazed earthenware cookware (such as traditional lead-glazed cazuelas and tagines) poses a documented heavy-metal leaching risk when underfired or exposed to acidic foods.
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Traditional folk remedies (boiling with water, vinegar, garlic, or lime) do not permanently neutralize unstable lead glazes; even nominally 'lead-free' ware can test positive if fired in kilns previously contaminated by lead glaze vapors.
sources: FDA Compliance Policy Guide Sec. 545.450 (fda.gov)
Digitalfire lead glaze technical reference (digitalfire.com)
Health Canada / CBC toxicological reports on Moroccan tagines (cbc.ca)
findings.value_or_range: Lead-fluxed earthenware fired ~900–1,000 °C; evaluated by FDA via 4% acetic acid 24-hour room-temperature leach test

findings.claim: Micaceous and burnished black earthenware (New Mexico Pueblo/Apachean micaceous clay; La Chamba, Colombia) achieves direct-flame thermal shock resistance through high concentrations of platy mica fired at low temperatures (<800–900 °C).
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Exact mica volume percentage varies by deposit (15% to >30% in NM Vadito Group residual clays; exact quantitative wt% of mica in La Chamba alluvial clay was not isolated in peer-reviewed XRD in our search, though museum/ethnoarchaeological sources confirm natural muscovite/biotite flakes). Keeping firing at 600–800 °C is essential because firing above ~900–1,000 °C dehydroxylates/fluxes mica and destroys the crack-deflecting cleavage planes. La Chamba's black finish is carbon-smudged reduction from organic smothering while hot, plus stone burnishing of a finer slip to curb permeability.
sources: Bronitsky & Hamer (1986), American Antiquity 51(1):89–101
Eiselt (Northern NM micaceous pottery, NIH / UNM / NM Archaeology)
Rye / Rice ceramic technology references & UC Berkeley La Chamba ethnoarchaeology studies
findings.value_or_range: Firing: 600–800 °C (typically 700–800 °C); Mica concentration: ~15–30%+ in NM micaceous pastes

findings.claim: Chinese Zisha (Yixing purple clay) is a Devonian sedimentary siltstone/mudstone sintered into a partially vitrified stoneware with a hierarchical dual-pore microstructure that makes it liquid-tight yet gas-permeable ('breathable').
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Reported porosity metrics vary between scholarly studies and tea-industry summaries, partly due to clay subtype (dense Zhuni vs. coarser Duanni) and 'open/water absorption' vs. 'total porosity' definitions: Wu et al. (2013) report ~2–5% water absorption and ~11–20%+ total porosity, whereas subtype surveys cite 3–12% water absorption (Zhuni <2–3%, Duanni 8–12%) and 3–14% apparent porosity. Crucially, standard Zisha teaware is NOT flameware: its high quartz content (~28–60%) and moderate CTE cause cracking on direct burner flames unless reformulated with coarse refractory grog or spodumene/petalite as shaguo casseroles.
sources: Wu et al. (2013), Ceramics International
Yang et al. (2021), Ceramics International 47(8)
Digitalfire thermal shock / flameware engineering notes (digitalfire.com)
findings.value_or_range: Raw mineralogy: 28–60% quartz, 30–50% illite/kaolinite/hydromica, 7–12%+ hematite; Firing: 1,100–1,200 °C (peak 1,150–1,180 °C); Water absorption: ~2–5% (up to 8–12% in coarse subtypes); Total porosity: ~11–20%+; Dual pores: ~0.2–0.5 µm intergranular + <10 nm matrix pores

findings.claim: Kaolin-rich stoneware and porcelain are defined industrially by high-temperature vitrification and near-zero open porosity, conferring high strength and chemical inertness but poor direct-flame thermal shock resistance.
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Thermal conductivity spans ~1.0–4.0 W/(m·K) for culinary stoneware/porcelain (20–50× lower than cast iron's ~50–80 W/(m·K)), creating steep wall thermal gradients on concentrated burners. Combined with a moderate CTE (~4.0–6.5 × 10^-6 K^-1), high elastic modulus, and lack of crack-blunting voids, standard vitrified stoneware/porcelain readily fractures on direct flame despite excelling in gradual oven or slow-cooker heating.
sources: ASTM C373 / ISO 10545-3 (austingallery.org, ResearchGate)
Digitalfire & ceramic engineering CTE tables (kyocera.com, digitalfire.com)
Thermtest & materials conductivity references (thermtest.com)
findings.value_or_range: Stoneware: 1,186–1,285 °C (Cone 5–10), water absorption ≤3% (typically 0.5–3%); Porcelain: 1,250–1,400 °C+ (Cone 10+), water absorption ≤0.5%; CTE: 4.0–6.5 × 10^-6 K^-1; Thermal conductivity: ~1.0–4.0 W/(m·K)

findings.claim: Lithium- and magnesium-aluminosilicate (LAS/MAS) flameware—using petalite, spodumene, cordierite, or beta-spodumene glass-ceramics—survives extreme direct-flame and freezer-to-oven shock primarily by engineering near-zero thermal expansion rather than relying on clay origin.
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Two distinct Japanese donabe mechanisms exist: Banko-yaki adds ~40–50% petalite (LiAlSi4O10 -> beta-spodumene on firing) to achieve low porosity and CTE ≤2.0 × 10^-6 K^-1, whereas traditional Iga-yaki (Nagatani-en) uses paleo-Lake Biwa organic-rich clay that burns out during firing to create insulating micro-porosity without petalite (exact peer-reviewed Iga porosity % was not found in English technical literature: LOW CONFIDENCE on exact figure). Corning Pyroceram 9608 (CorningWare, beta-spodumene glass-ceramic) achieves 0–2.5 × 10^-6 K^-1 CTE and ~2.05 W/(m·K) conductivity (distinct from cordierite Pyroceram 9606 radomes at ~5.7 × 10^-6 K^-1). Emile Henry Flame claims pure Burgundy clay without synthetic spodumene/petalite/cordierite and uses an intentionally micro-crazing stress-relief glaze, but exact mineral processing is a proprietary trade secret (LOW CONFIDENCE on exact phase composition).
sources: Corning / NIST / NASA / Thermtest Pyroceram 9608 datasheets (nist.gov, nasa.gov, thermtest.com)
Ceramic engineering CTE tables & cordierite/petalite papers (NIH, ResearchGate, ceramic-science.com)
Mie Prefecture / Banko & Iga donabe technical literature (ResearchGate, Nagatani-en/Saikai)
Emile Henry technical disclosures (emilehenryusa.com, everythingkitchens.com)
findings.value_or_range: Petalite-bearing bodies CTE: -0.5 to 1.0 × 10^-6 K^-1 (Banko-yaki ~40–50% petalite -> ≤2.0 × 10^-6 K^-1); Cordierite CTE: 0.5–2.0 × 10^-6 K^-1; Pyroceram 9608 CTE: ~0–2.5 × 10^-6 K^-1, conductivity ~2.05 W/(m·K)

findings.claim: 'Volcanic clay' is a commercial marketing label rather than a mineralogical clay classification; genuine volcanic-derived ceramics rely either on weathered alteration clays (smectite, allophane, halloysite) or non-plastic volcanic rock tempers/fluxes (basalt, pumice, scoria), while modern Korean flameproof ttukbaegi actually rely on added petalite.
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Fresh lava, basalt, and pumice have zero plasticity and cannot be formed alone. In Korea, traditional onggi and ttukbaegi are made from regional illite-chlorite-kaolinite secondary clays + quartz/feldspar (40–56% SiO2, 13–25% Al2O3, 4–8% Fe2O3) fired at 1,100–1,200 °C with ~10.8–38.2% porosity depending on firing temperature and pore-formers (such as charcoal); Jeju volcanic scoria ('songyi') is researched as a porous iron/magnesium-rich aggregate/flux fired at 900–1,200 °C. Modern 'crack-free/0%-absorption' Korean ttukbaegi achieve stovetop durability by blending imported petalite and firing >1,250 °C—not from volcanic stone.
sources: Journal of the Korean Ceramic Society (Katsuki et al., jkcs.or.kr) & Semantic Scholar on Onggi porosity
MDPI & JKCS studies on Jeju volcanic scoria ceramics (mdpi.com, jkcs.or.kr)
Soil/clay mineralogy references on volcanic ash weathering (Britannica, ResearchGate, IntechOpen)
Korean flameware/ttukbaegi petalite manufacturer technical disclosures (aardvarkclay.com, gochujar.com)
findings.value_or_range: Onggi matrix: 40–56% SiO2, 13–25% Al2O3, 4–8% Fe2O3; Firing: 1,100–1,200 °C; Onggi porosity: 20.9–38.2% at 1,100 °C dropping to 10.8–30.9% at 1,200 °C; Jeju scoria composites sintered at 900–1,200 °C (red clay-scoria ~950 °C)

findings.claim: During cooking, the geographic or trade name of a clay matters far less than three interacting engineering variables: (1) firing temperature/vitrification, (2) open porosity, and (3) thermal expansion management across body, temper, and glaze.
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Per Kingery (1955) and Hasselman (1969–1970) thermal-shock theory plus Skibo's behavioral pottery studies, cookware faces an inherent engineering trade-off: high open porosity and coarse platy/mineral temper blunt cracks and raise thermal shock survival (e.g., micaceous ware, Iga donabe, terracotta), but increase liquid/oil/soap absorption and reduce mechanical strength; conversely, high-fired vitrification (stoneware/porcelain) seals pores and raises strength, but makes bodies brittle under direct-flame gradients unless CTE is engineered near zero with petalite or cordierite. Glaze fit also governs performance: glazes must have a slightly lower CTE than the body to remain in compression; tensile crazing can reduce ceramic strength by up to 300–400% and create sanitation/leaching pathways. Furthermore, the 573 °C alpha-to-beta quartz inversion creates sharp volumetric stress whenever high-quartz bodies are heated rapidly.
sources: Kingery (1955) & Hasselman (1969–1970) thermal shock equations (MDPI, Sciopen, ResearchGate)
Skibo & Schiffer pottery performance trade-offs (ResearchGate, tandfonline.com)
Digitalfire glaze fit, compression/crazing, and 573 °C quartz inversion guides (digitalfire.com)
findings.value_or_range: Quartz inversion at 573 °C; tensile glaze crazing can reduce ceramic structural strength by up to 300–400%

findings.claim: Clay cookware's gentle, even heating arises from low thermal conductivity and high surface emissivity—not from unique 'far-infrared' wavelengths exclusive to special clays.
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: By Planck's and Wien's displacement laws, emission wavelength depends on temperature, not clay mineralogy: any pan at 100–250 °C emits mid-to-far IR (~5–20 µm), and IR penetrates only microscopic fractions of a millimeter into food. However, ceramics do exhibit high surface emissivity (ε ≈ 0.90–0.95 vs. <0.1 for polished bare aluminum/steel) alongside low thermal conductivity (0.15–4 W/(m·K) vs. 50–80 W/(m·K) for cast iron), creating high thermal inertia and inward radiative warmth without hot-spot scorching.
sources: Thermodynamics (Planck's & Wien's laws) & ceramic thermal conductivity data (thermtest.com, ceramics.org)
Ceramic emissivity vs. polished metal analyses (yakimono.or.jp, soonear.me)
findings.value_or_range: IR peak at 100–250 °C: ~5–20 µm regardless of material; Ceramic emissivity ε: ~0.90–0.95 (polished metal <0.1); Clay conductivity: 0.15–4.0 W/(m·K) vs. cast iron 50–80 W/(m·K)

myths_checked: Myth: 'Volcanic clay' is a distinct natural clay mineral that lets pots be shaped straight from lava rock. Reality: Raw basalt/pumice/lava has zero plasticity; commercial 'volcanic clay' cookware either uses weathered volcanic soils (smectite/allophane/halloysite), basalt/scoria temper, or standard clays doped with petalite/sol-gel coatings.

Myth: Clay pots (or volcanic/Zisha/donabe pots) emit special 'far-infrared' frequencies that metals cannot, cooking food from the inside out. Reality: Per Wien's Law, any surface at 100–250 °C emits ~5–20 µm mid-to-far IR, which penetrates only fractions of a millimeter; clay's real advantage is high emissivity (0.90–0.95 vs <0.1 for shiny metal) plus low thermal conductivity (0.15–4 W/m·K) that buffers hot spots.

Myth: Traditional curing (boiling with vinegar, garlic, or lime) seals or neutralizes lead in low-fired glazed terracotta cazuelas or tagines. Reality: FDA testing confirms household curing does not stop lead leaching when a glaze is underfired or unstable; acidic foods accelerate leaching.

Myth: All famous traditional Chinese Zisha or vitrified French/European stoneware is inherently stovetop/direct-flame safe. Reality: Standard Zisha teaware (high quartz, ~2–5% water absorption) and standard vitrified stoneware/porcelain will crack under direct burner gradients unless specifically formulated with low-CTE minerals (petalite, spodumene, cordierite), heavy platy/coarse temper, or proprietary stress-relief engineering.

Myth: Porous cookware is always weaker against heat than dense high-fired stoneware. Reality: For direct-flame thermal shock, controlled open porosity and platy mica or coarse temper actually outperform dense vitrified stoneware by blunting crack propagation and lowering elastic modulus (Hasselman theory), at the trade-off of higher water absorption and lower mechanical impact strength.
